extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (USPTO examiners, search/classification staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for locating, interpreting, citing, and treating foreign patent documents and related family members as prior art or references during U.S. patent examination, including how to read country-specific publication data and INID bibliographic codes. Covers priority claims, translations, family relationships, and sources for locating corresponding documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family of patents (definition and treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of patents issued in different countries for the same invention is referred to as a family of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because separate patents must be obtained in each country, corresponding specifications in a family are generally identical in substance but may be translations, combined filings, continuation-in-part, or may have disclosure diminished or increased to meet national requirements. Examiners should verify whether earlier related documents in a family include the subject matter necessary for a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paris Convention right of priority (requirements and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application is filed in a Paris-Convention country, a later-filed application for the same invention in another Paris country within one year will be entitled to the benefit of the filing date of the first application upon fulfillment of various conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents or published specifications of the later filing countries are required to specify that priority has been claimed and to give the country, date, and number of the priority application; this information aids locating any patent based on the priority application. See MPEP §213 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing foreign language specifications and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate or substantially duplicate foreign language specifications (and translations) may both exist and can be cited as references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is possible to cite a foreign language specification as a reference while also citing an English language version with a later date as a convenient translation if the latter is in fact a translation. Questions about content in such cases must be settled based on the specification which was used as the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check foreign priority/publication when U.S. reference claims foreign priority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a U.S. patent or U.S. published application being considered as a reference claims the priority of a previously filed foreign application, determine if the foreign application has issued or been published to see if there is an earlier date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should check foreign documents because a foreign patent or publication may have an earlier printed publication date than the U.S. document; that earlier date can affect 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections. Whether a foreign priority application filing date can serve as an 'effectively filed date' under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) is governed by 35 U.S.C. 102(d) (see MPEP § 2154.01(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of earlier family members as prior art when outside convention year
rubrics_metrics.description: When a later application is filed outside the Paris Convention year from an earlier application, the earlier application may be prior art to the later application if the earlier has been published or issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicate specifications published without indication of the relationship can occur; these may be detected when two copies come together in the same subclass. Examiners should detect duplicates and verify dates and disclosures of the related documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify earlier related document contains necessary subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Related documents in a family usually have identical disclosures but sometimes contain differences in claims or minor specification differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should always verify that the earlier related document also includes the subject matter necessary for the rejection before relying on it as a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for locating corresponding patents and publications
rubrics_metrics.description: There are commercial and public resources available to locate corresponding patents and publications from other patent offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful sources include the Derwent World Patents Index (DWPI), the International Patent Documentation Center (INPADOC), Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) patent abstracts, Global Dossier Public Access, and WIPO-CASE. Examiners may consult STIC staff for access to Chemical Abstracts or for help obtaining documents not covered by the country table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of dates displayed on face of foreign patent documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner is not required to prove dates or specifications of foreign patents/applications or official journals when the Office has copies in its possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office copies constitute prima facie evidence under 28 U.S.C. 1745. An applicant may rebut by competent evidence, but such disputes seldom arise. The date of receipt of copies by the Office, as shown by Office records or stamps, need only be stated by the examiner when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use country-specific document table
rubrics_metrics.description: Each row in the table contains information on one or more distinct patent documents from a specified country available as a reference under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and 102(b) or 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several distinct documents are included within a common box, they are related documents published at different stages. The top listed document is the one 'published' first. Once the country/publishing organization is determined, the examiner should locate the document name in the table to determine the correct citation date to use and then verify whether an earlier related document with an earlier date is available and contains the needed subject matter. Separate rows are provided for different patent types when countries issue more than one type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country-specific publication/name/date practices (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different countries use different document names and different 'date' conventions to indicate the date for citation purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the table: EP — printing of application occurs 18 months after priority date; EP dates are day/month/year. FR — 'date of laying open application' is usually earliest possible date, occurs 18 months after filing or priority but can occur earlier at applicant request. DE — multiple printings (including a 'DD' series) occur as examination proceeds; DE dates are day/month/year. JP — Japanese application publication dates use the year of the Emperor and require conversion to Gregorian calendar (add 1925 for years prior to 1989, add 1988 for years after 1988). Examiners should use the document-specific 'type of date' indicated in the table for citation purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of Japanese imperial years to Gregorian dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese patent application publications show the date in Arabic numerals indicating (in order) the year of the reign of the Emperor, the month, and the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convert the Japanese year of the Emperor to the Western calendar year: for years prior to 1989 add 1925 (e.g., 40.3.6 = March 6, 1965); for years after 1988 add 1988.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of INID codes to identify bibliographic data on first page (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: INID Codes (Internationally agreed Numbers for the Identification of (bibliographic) Data) indicate various bibliographic data on the first page without knowledge of the language used or laws applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INID codes are used by most patent offices and applied to U.S. patents since Aug 4, 1970. The MPEP lists INID codes and minimum required elements (based on WIPO Standard ST.9). Important groupings and examples: (10) identification of patent document; (11) patent number; (12) plain language designation of kind of document; (13) kind code per ST.16; (19) ST.3 code of publishing office; (20s) data concerning application and languages (21–26); (30s) priority data (31–34) and presentation notes; (40s) dates of making available to the public (41–47); (50s) technical information including IPC and title (51,54,56,57,58); (60s) references to related domestic or prior documents (61–68); (70s) parties (71,72,73,75–76); (80s–90s) conventions and PCT/SPC-related codes (81–98). Follow the specific notes (presentation, language codes, minimum data elements) provided for each code in the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation rules and notes for INID-coded data
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific presentation rules apply when using INID codes (e.g., how to present multiple application/publication data sets, language codes, and minimum data elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When codes (31,32,33) or (86,87,96,97) refer to multiple regional/PCT applications, present each set so they are clearly distinguishable (e.g., on single lines, grouped with blank lines between sets). Indicate languages with two-letter ISO 639 codes, and countries with WIPO ST.3 two-letter codes. Some codes are minimum data elements for patent documents (marked °°). For SPCs and other special cases, follow the specific notes (e.g., code (68) for SPC basic patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: INID codes and minimum bibliographic data for industrial designs
rubrics_metrics.description: INID codes for industrial designs are similar but not identical to patent INID codes and are intended to identify bibliographic data on the first page of design documents (based on WIPO Standard ST.80).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key codes include (10) registration/renewal data; (11) serial number; (12) plain language designation of kind; (15) date of registration/renewal; (21–24) application data and exhibition priority; (30–33) priority under Paris Convention (31–33 present together or use 30); (40s) dates of making information available to the public (43–45); (50s) miscellaneous information (51 — Locarno classification; 54 — designation of article/product; 55 — reproduction/drawing; 57 — description of characteristic features); (60s–70s) references and parties (60,62,66,71–73). Minimum data elements for design documents are noted (°°). Present country/classification codes using WIPO ST.3 where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining which document date to use for citation purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The table indicates, for each country and document type, which date is used for citation purposes (e.g., date published, date application made available to the public, date of laying open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must use the 'type of date' designated in the table for citation. For related groups, the top-listed document is the one published first; check whether an earlier related document in the group has an earlier date that is appropriate for use as a reference. If an earlier effective date is important to a rejection and not readily apparent from the face of the document, consult STIC staff who may attempt to obtain further information.
